header:
Determination of Ionic Constituents
During the preparation of K_3[Al(C_2O_4)_3]·3H_2O crystals, some Cr^3+ ions were introduced to replace Al^3+. The following titration experiments were designed to determine the Al and Cr contents of the crystal sample. Titration experiment I: dissolve a 0.5062 g crystal sample in water and transfer it to a 100 mL conical flask. Add a buffer to adjust the pH, then add a solution containing 2.024×10^-3 mol of EDTA. Heat at a gentle boil for 10 min, cool, and add indicator A. Titrate to the endpoint with 0.09142 mol/L standard Zn^2+ solution; 10.40 mL of the standard Zn^2+ solution is consumed. Titration experiment II: dissolve a separate 2.5015 g crystal sample in water and transfer it to a 100 mL conical flask. Acidify with sulfuric acid, add excess (NH_4)_2S_2O_8 and a catalytic amount of Ag^+, then heat at boiling for 10 min. Cool, add indicator B, and titrate with 0.1515 mol/L standard Fe^2+ solution; 17.94 mL of the standard Fe^2+ solution is consumed. Note: assume that the two samples have the same composition and that impurities do not participate in the titration reactions. Report calculated results to 3 significant figures.

header:
Lithium Redox-Flow Battery
A lithium redox-flow battery based on redox-targeting reactions is shown below. Redox targeting links an active material to an electrode by introducing into the electrolyte a highly soluble redox mediator paired with that active material. This approach both circumvents the solubility limitation of the active material and allows low-solubility active materials to be stored in tanks.

header_images.description: Schematic of an electrochemical flow apparatus. At the center is a battery stack composed of multiple plate-like layers, with blue outer plates and black and green layers between them. The left blue plate is labeled “+” and the right blue plate “-”. A wire at the top connects to a glowing light bulb; \(e\) is labeled above the wire, and an arrow shows electron transfer from the blue plate labeled “-” to the blue plate labeled “+”. Blue tubing connects the left vessel to the central stack and forms a circulation loop through a bottom pump labeled \(\mathrm{Pump}\). The circulation direction is: blue plate labeled “+” → lower blue tubing → \(\mathrm{Pump}\) → bottom of the left vessel (\(\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}\)) → \(\mathrm{LiFePO_4}\) → upper part of the left vessel (\(\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}\)) → upper blue tubing → blue plate on the side labeled “+”. To the right of the stack is a cylindrical vessel containing a pale-yellow liquid and a cylindrical material labeled \(\mathrm{LiTi_2(PO_4)_3}\). \(\mathrm{S_2^{2-}}\) is labeled above it and \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\) below it. header:
Preparation of a Dinuclear Ti Complex
In benzene solution, 10.5 mmol of TiBr_4 is mixed with 5 mmol of B_2(NMe_2)_4. A dark-red solution forms immediately, followed by a brown precipitate. The reaction mixture is stirred vigorously at room temperature for 5 h, after which the volatile components are removed under vacuum and passed successively through cold traps at -22 ℃ and -196 ℃. The -196 ℃ trap contains the benzene solvent, whereas the substance collected in the -22 ℃ trap is identified as B(NMe_2)_3. The remaining liquid is removed by distillation, and the insoluble solid is washed with DCM to give a sample whose principal component is X. A 219.7 mg portion of the sample is treated with 25 % sulfuric acid solution, immediately producing a dark-purple solution with no gas evolution at room temperature. Addition of sufficient NaOH solution, from which dissolved air has been removed, to this dark-purple solution produces a blue-black precipitate that gradually evolves gas and is ultimately converted into a white precipitate. On the basis of IR, 1H-NMR, magnetic-moment, and other studies, a structure is proposed for X. In this structure, only one type of coordinating atom and two types of ligands surround Ti. The B-containing ligand, denoted L, is bidentate, and the three atoms bonded to each B atom are all different. The relative molecular mass of the molecule is 1114.3 g/mol.

How Well Do You Really Know Carbon-Phosphorus Double Bonds?
In studying organic chemistry, we seem to restrict our understanding of the reactivity of carbon-phosphorus double bonds to their “metathesis” reactions with carbon-oxygen double bonds. header: Problem 6 Exploring Our Little Broken Planet. Rocks are generally mixtures of one or more minerals and can be classified as igneous, metamorphic, or sedimentary. Geological processes can transform each type into the others. Igneous rocks form when magma cools. Magma is a complex mixture without a fixed melting point; melting occurs over a temperature range, beginning at the solidus and becoming complete at the liquidus. Most rocks undergo partial melting. During magma cooling and crystallization, changes in physical and chemical conditions cause minerals of different compositions to crystallize in sequence. Consequently, the solid and residual melt often have different chemical compositions. This phenomenon is called chemical differentiation. Temperature, chemical composition, and gravity are important factors affecting chemical differentiation. Metamorphic rocks form when pre-existing rocks in the crust—igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic—undergo changes in mineral composition, texture, structure, and chemical composition under the influence of temperature, pressure, and chemically active fluids. Metamorphism generally occurs below the solidus temperature of the rock (600-1000 ℃), so melting does not occur in the great majority of cases; pressure, however, has no strict upper limit.

The diagram contains a curve labeled solidus, which is the thickest curve, a curve labeled liquidus to its right, and several nearly parallel thin curves between them. A rock has high crystallinity if its mineral grains are large and well crystallized, with regular and complete particle arrangements and few defects or disorders; otherwise, it has low crystallinity. State whether intrusive or extrusive rocks have higher crystallinity and briefly explain why. (No more than 50 words.)

header: Problem 1 Minerals and Chemistry. In the 18 century, Austrian chemist F. J. Müller discovered a substance X resembling antimony in a gold-bearing ore. It was not until 16 years later that German mineralogist M. H. Klaproth formally discovered and named it. Roasting an X-containing mineral A in air gives B and elemental silver. Theoretically, roasting each 1.000 g of A produces 0.628 g of silver.

subquestions.text_open:
It is known that element $X=Te$, mineral $A=Ag_2Te$, and product $B=TeO_2$.
1-2 B can be further converted into other compounds of X. (i) B dissolves in a concentrated solution of C to give a solution containing D, while base G is also formed. D reacts with E in a 1:2 ratio, precipitating elemental X and producing C and F. (ii) B reacts with base G to form H. A solution in glacial acetic acid of the acid corresponding to the anion of excess H reacts with F in a 1:4 ratio to give the X-containing compound I and the X-free compound J. Reaction of I with G precipitates elemental X and also forms F and H. (iii) Under acidic conditions, B reacts with hydrogen peroxide to give K. K is reduced by a common monoprotic strong acid L, producing B, X, and elemental M. Interestingly, M reacts with F to form J, a reaction commonly used to titrate M in analytical chemistry. C is a binary compound, and C, D, E, F, H, I, and J are all 2:1 salts. Determine the formulas of compounds D, E, I, and J.

By a brief calculation, determine whether a mixture of K and concentrated hydrochloric acid can dissolve gold at room temperature.

header: Problem 1: The Immortal Red Dragon. The development of alchemy depended on the joint investigations of scholars in China and abroad. In Tiangong Kaiwu, Song Yingxing recorded a method for purifying the “Red Dragon.” Low-purity “Red Dragon” was first “calcined together for five double-hours” in a sealed iron vessel to obtain a silvery-white elemental metal that is liquid at room temperature. The metal was then reacted in the proportion “one jin of metal to two jin of shitingzhi (a nonmetallic element),” yielding “fourteen liang of vermilion and three liang five qian of secondary vermilion.” Both “vermilion” and “secondary vermilion” are high-purity forms of the “Red Dragon.”

1-2 Throughout the history of alchemy, many scholars explored the chemical properties of the “Red Dragon.” Because it is chemically stable, subduing the immortal “Red Dragon” was a longstanding goal of alchemists. (i) Boiling a mixture of “wood ash” and “lime” gives strongly basic “caustic potash.” Boiling this with excess sulfur produces a dark-red mixed solution called “liver of sulfur.” When the “Red Dragon” is placed in this solution, it “completely merges with the red holy water.” Adding acid generates foul-smelling “dragon's breath” and instantly turns the originally clear liquid turbid (reaction 1). After the reaction, a large amount of soft, pale yellow-brown powder remains at the bottom. (ii) The “Green Lion” is a salt with formula mass 278.02. When strongly heated in a furnace, it first releases clear water and then “roars” out pungent “white smoke,” which condenses into a highly corrosive viscous liquid called “oil of vitriol” (reaction 2). Heating “oil of vitriol” with “saltpeter,” a potassium salt, produces dense “red fumes” that condense into slightly yellow “strong water.” Adding “sal ammoniac,” an ammonium salt, to the “strong water” gives the “King's Sword,” meaning aqua regia. When the King's Sword pierces the “Red Dragon,” it dies amid “red fumes”; its body is completely consumed into clear water, leaving only “yellow grease” floating on the surface (reaction 3). The “yellow grease” is the same substance as shitingzhi. Write the equations for reactions 1-3. Note: reaction 1 comprises two reactions, and reaction 2 is the overall reaction by which the “Green Lion” forms “oil of vitriol.”

header:
Determination of Sulfur Dioxide in Wine
The sulfur dioxide content of a wine sample is determined spectrophotometrically as follows. I. Construct a calibration curve. Accurately transfer 0.00 mL, 0.20 mL, 0.50 mL, 1.00 mL, 2.00 mL, and 3.00 mL of sulfur dioxide working standard solutions (containing 0.0 μg, 2.0 μg, 5.0 μg, 10.0 μg, 20.0 μg, and 30.0 μg sulfur dioxide, respectively) into 25 mL stoppered test tubes, and add formaldehyde-buffered absorbing solution to 10.00 mL. Then add, in sequence, 0.5 mL of 3 g/L ammonium sulfamate solution, 0.5 mL of 1.5 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution, and 1.0 mL of 0.5 g/L pararosaniline hydrochloride solution (structure shown below). Mix thoroughly and allow to stand for 20 min. Measure the absorbance of each standard solution at 579 nm using a UV–visible spectrophotometer. The following data are obtained:

| $\text{SO}_2$ content $m / \mu\text{g}$ | 0.0 | 2.0 | 5.0 | 10.0 | 20.0 | 30.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Absorbance $A$ | 0.003 | 0.062 | 0.159 | 0.312 | 0.618 | 0.928 |

II. Accurately weigh 0.5000 g of the wine sample and add formaldehyde-buffered absorbing solution to 100 mL. After shaking for 2 h, take 10 mL of the solution and perform the spectrophotometric determination as in Step I. Repeat the measurement three times; the absorbances A’ are 0.637, 0.638, and 0.635. In China, the required sulfur dioxide content of alcoholic beverages is below $0.2500 \ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$. Take the density of the wine to be $0.9 \ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. header:
Problem 1 Peierls's Wondrous Gift
In the 18 century, Austrian mineralogist Müller von Reichenstein discovered a new substance while studying a gold ore. It had a silvery-white metallic luster but was brittle and a poor conductor; it burned with a blue flame and gave off an unusual odor resembling rotten radishes. German chemist Martin Klaproth later confirmed that it was a new element and named it after the Latin word for Earth. Interestingly, another member of the same group discovered decades later was named after the Moon to complement Earth. This element, denoted E, can be obtained by reduction of either its oxide A or its sodium oxoacid salt B; E has the same oxidation state in A and B. An early preparation heated B with carbon black. The simple hydride C of E is a foul-smelling, highly unstable gas whose aqueous solution is weakly acidic. Passing C into $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ solution gives a black precipitate. Another oxide D of E is an orange solid. When D dissolves in concentrated aqueous NaOH, the resulting anhydrous sodium salt contains 46.64% E by mass.

subquestions.text_open: 1-2-1 Write the equation for heating B with carbon black to obtain elemental E.
1-2-3 Write the equation for dissolution of D in concentrated aqueous NaOH.

1-4-1 Structural studies of $\alpha$-E show infinite one-dimensional zigzag chains in which each E atom bonds to its two neighboring E atoms, forming continuous $(E)_n$ chains with $n\rightarrow\infty$. Elemental halogen X is widely used for surgical disinfection. E and X form F, G, and H with E:X ratios of 1:1, 2:1, and 1:4, respectively. F retains the $(E)_n$ chain. Both E and X have two chemical environments, each in a 1:1 ratio. The coordination numbers of the two E atoms are in a 3:4 ratio, and one X atom forms only one covalent bond to E. G can be viewed as portions of two long F chains joined by additional E-E bonds to form an infinite six-membered-ring structure, and the E coordination numbers in G are the same as in F. H exists as a tetramer with two E environments, and every E atom is six-coordinate. Give SMILES descriptions of the structural motifs of F and G.
1-4-2 Give the SMILES structure of the H tetramer.

header:
Lithium or Sodium?
Balancing fluctuations in renewable-electricity generation through electrochemical energy storage is essential to achieving carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality goals. Lithium-ion batteries dominate the market, but constraints on lithium resources have stimulated research into sodium-ion batteries. Their operating principles are similar, yet their material structures and performance differ substantially. This problem considers two representative layered-oxide cathodes.

subquestions.text_open:
6.2 The following electrochemical data are given. NCM811 has an average discharge voltage of 3.8 V versus metallic lithium and an actual reversible specific capacity of $200\,\mathrm{mAh\cdot g^{-1}}$. The P2 sodium material has an average discharge voltage of 3.2 V versus metallic sodium and an actual reversible specific capacity of $130\,\mathrm{mAh\cdot g^{-1}}$. The volumetric energy density is $E_v=\rho\times C\times U$, where $\rho$ is density, $C$ specific capacity, and $U$ average voltage.
6.2.1 Calculate the theoretical volumetric energy density of each cathode and their ratio $\lambda$ (lithium-based/sodium-based).

The diffusion coefficient D of ions in a layered material and the temperature T obey the Arrhenius equation. For P2-type $Na_{0.67}Ni_{0.33}Mn_{0.67}O_2$, the experimentally measured pre-exponential factor is $D_0 = 5.0 × 10^{-4} cm^2·s^{-1}$ and the activation energy is E_a = 0.35 eV. header:
Material-Balance Analysis of an Electrolytic Process
"If this silvery-white lightweight metal could be produced on a large scale at low cost, transportation and building structures would undergo a qualitative transformation." In the late 19th century, industry fiercely competed to develop a method for producing this lightweight metal. At almost the same time, chemists Charles M. Hall and Paul Héroult independently proposed, on opposite sides of the Atlantic, a high-temperature molten-salt electrolysis route: a reddish-brown ore A (whose principal component is A') is purified and then electrolytically reduced in a molten-salt bath to obtain the silvery-white metal B, thereby laying the foundation of the modern metallurgical industry for B. Natural ore A is usually reddish brown and often contains silicon dioxide impurities. During electrolysis, the mineral flux C is added to lower the melting point of the system, and a carbonaceous anode is used. The anode is continuously consumed, releasing gas D. Industrial electrolytic cells normally operate at atmospheric pressure and at approximately 955℃. Before Hall-Héroult electrolysis, ore A must be purified by the Bayer process. This process mainly comprises the following steps: first, crushed ore A is stirred with a 30 wt% NaOH solution at 473 K and 3.5 MPa for 2 h, converting it into the soluble complex E; the solution is then cooled to 320 K, seeded with particles approximately 75 μm in size (50 g·L^{-1}), and allowed to stand for 48 h, precipitating F with a relatively narrow particle-size distribution that facilitates subsequent calcination; finally, F is calcined in air at 1370 K for 6 h to regenerate high-purity A'. When mineral flux C is the principal component of the molten-salt bath, the bath usually contains two key substances: solid G, which must be replenished periodically, and compound H. Solid G is added periodically to maintain their molar ratio in the bath. If $Na_2CO_3$ impurity enters the bath, $Na_2CO_3$ reacts with G, releasing a small amount of gas D and producing compound H, which remains soluble in the molten-salt bath, together with another by-product. Define the bath ratio as BR = n(H) / n(G) = 2.50

subquestions.text_open: 1.2 On a certain day, 15.0 kg of $Na_2CO_3$ impurity enters the molten-salt bath. Assume that all H produced dissolves in the bath and all D escapes. 1.2.1 Calculate the mass of A' additionally produced by the side reaction that day.
1.2.2 Calculate the additional mass of G that should be added that day to restore BR to 2.50.

header:
Kjeldahl Nitrogen Determination
Determination of nitrogen content has long been an important topic in analytical chemistry. In 1883, the Danish chemist Johan G.C.T. Kjeldahl invented the Kjeldahl method. The method mainly comprises digestion, alkalization, and titration: sulfuric-acid digestion converts the nitrogen in a sample into an ammonium salt; alkalization releases ammonia by distillation; and the absorbed ammonia is quantified indirectly by acid-base titration. The organic nitrogen content of a solid sample is to be determined. Answer the following questions based on the procedures described.

Swirl gently, place a small funnel in the flask mouth, and set the flask at an angle of 45° on an asbestos gauze with a small opening. Heat slowly. When the contents turn black and foaming has completely ceased, increase the heat to keep the liquid gently boiling. After the liquid becomes blue-green, clear, and transparent, continue heating for another $1 \ \mathrm{h}$. Remove the Kjeldahl flask and cool it to room temperature. Carefully add $20 \ \mathrm{mL}$ of water, quantitatively transfer the contents to a $100 \ \mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask, rinse the inner wall of the Kjeldahl flask with a small amount of water, and combine the rinsings in the volumetric flask. Dilute to volume with water, mix, and reserve for use. Conduct a blank experiment in parallel. From the apparatus shown below, select the Kjeldahl flask suitable for digestion. header:
Semiconductors and Electrochemistry
Semiconductors are materials whose electrical conductivity at room temperature lies between that of conductors and insulators. Common semiconductor materials include silicon, germanium, and gallium arsenide. Based on band theory and Fermi statistics, doping with group V or group III elements, or with other materials that can donate electrons (donors) or accept electrons (acceptors), can regulate the Fermi level and carrier concentration of a semiconductor and thereby its various properties. Semiconductor carriers generally comprise electrons and holes. In this problem, involving an n-type semiconductor in which electrons are the majority carriers, only electrons need be considered. Nonuniform doping can create a carrier-concentration gradient in a semiconductor. The resulting diffusion causes charge separation and a built-in electric field; the built-in field opposes diffusion until equilibrium is reached. This is fundamentally similar to the electrochemical picture in which a chemical-potential difference drives charge transfer, which in turn produces a potential difference that opposes further charge transfer, ultimately establishing an electrode potential at equilibrium. By comparing a concentration-gradient-doped semiconductor with the electromotive force of an electrochemical concentration cell, this problem explores the universality of diffusion-electric-field equilibrium.
7.1 Built-in electric field and diffusion equilibrium in a semiconductor
Consider an n-type semiconductor at temperature T = 300 K with electron concentration varying with position x as $n(x)=N_{d0}\exp(-x/L)$. Here $N_{d0}=1\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, $L=0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, $D_n=225\ \mathrm{cm}^2\mathrm{/s}$, $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and $k=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$. These quantities are, respectively, the donor concentration at x = 0 (which, under the approximation used here, may be regarded as the electron concentration at x = 0), characteristic length, electron diffusion coefficient, elementary charge, and Boltzmann constant.

header:
Problem 2 Schrödinger's Hydrogen-Atom Model
The year 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the publication of Schrödinger's wave mechanics. In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the electron is a particle moving in a fixed circular orbit. Schrödinger's wave mechanics instead treats the electron as having wave-particle duality and therefore as unable to possess simultaneously definite position and momentum. In wave mechanics, the state of motion of a particle is described by a wavefunction. In general, a wavefunction depends on time and position; if it is time-independent, it reduces to a function of position. The wavefunction itself does not directly give definite values of physical quantities such as position or momentum. Rather, it contains information about their probability distributions. Appropriate mathematical operations on the wavefunction yield the probability of finding the particle at a given location, the possible values of its momentum, and the energy of the system.
How is the wavefunction obtained? A fundamental postulate of quantum mechanics is that the wavefunction satisfies the Schrödinger equation. This equation is a partial differential equation, and its solutions are wavefunctions. Thus, one first writes the Schrödinger equation for an electron, solves it for a wavefunction, and then uses the resulting wavefunction to determine information about position, momentum, energy, and other quantities.
If the potential-energy distribution in space is time-independent, the wavefunction is a function only of position and the equation is called the time-independent Schrödinger equation. For a hydrogen atom, for example, the nucleus may be approximated as fixed; the equation describing the electron is then time-independent, and the electron wavefunction depends on its position coordinates. Position may be expressed in Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$, but spherical polar coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$ are often used. The physical meanings of $r,\theta,\phi$ are shown below, with $r>0,0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,0 \leq \phi \leq 2\pi$.
The time-independent Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom is
$$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi(r,\theta,\phi)-\frac{Ke^2}{r}\psi(r,\theta,\phi)=E\psi(r,\theta,\phi)$$
where $\nabla^2$ is the Laplace operator, which in spherical polar coordinates is
$$\nabla^2=\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2}+\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^2}\left(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}+\frac{1}{\tan\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}+\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \phi^2}\right)$$
Here $m$ is the electron mass, $K$ is the electrostatic-force constant, and $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant. $E$ is called the energy eigenvalue, or simply the electron energy. Although the electron's momentum and position are uncertain, its energy is definite.
Note: $\partial$ denotes partial differentiation. If $f$ is a function of $x,y$, then $\frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}$ is defined as the derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ while the independent variable $y$ is held constant:
$$\frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}=\lim_{\Delta x\to 0}\frac{f(x+\Delta x,y)-f(x,y)}{\Delta x}$$
When $f$ is independent of $y$, so that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=0$ identically, $f$ becomes a single-variable function of $x$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}$. A differentiation formula that may be useful is $(x^{\alpha}e^{kx})'=(kx^{\alpha}+\alpha x^{\alpha-1})e^{kx}$.
The time-independent Schrödinger equation for hydrogen has infinitely many solutions. Certain solutions correspond to the atomic orbitals of hydrogen; each orbital is described by a particular wavefunction. The wavefunctions for the orbitals in the first two shells are listed below. 1s: $\psi_{1s}(r,\theta,\phi)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi a_0^3}}e^{-r/a_0}$; 2s: $\psi_{2s}(r,\theta,\phi)=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi a_0^3}}\left(2-\frac{r}{a_0}\right)e^{-r/(2a_0)}$; $ 2p_x$: $\psi_{2p_x}(r,\theta,\phi)=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi a_0^3}}\left(\frac{r}{a_0}\right)e^{-r/(2a_0)}\sin\theta\cos\phi$; $ 2p_y$: $\psi_{2p_y}(r,\theta,\phi)=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi a_0^3}}\left(\frac{r}{a_0}\right)e^{-r/(2a_0)}\sin\theta\sin\phi$; $ 2p_z$: $\psi_{2p_z}(r,\theta,\phi)=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi a_0^3}}\left(\frac{r}{a_0}\right)e^{-r/(2a_0)}\cos\theta$. Here $a_0=\frac{\hbar^2}{Ke^2m}=52.9\text{pm}$ is the Bohr radius.

header: The history of first-generation glucose biosensors dates to 1962, when Clark and Lyons at Cincinnati Children's Hospital immobilized a thin layer of glucose oxidase, GOD, on an oxygen electrode behind a semipermeable membrane permeable only to $O_2$. Blood glucose is determined from the resulting change in oxygen-electrode potential.

One O atom has coordinates (0.222, 0.5, 0.205), both Ni and Na occupy vertex or face-center positions, and the unit-cell parameters are a = 5.33 Å, b = 2.86 Å, c = 5.59 Å, and β = 110.5°. 5.2.1 Before distortion, the structure follows a close-packing model: O forms the closest-packed array, while alternating Na and Ni layers occupy octahedral holes in the O array. Use ABC for the close-packed O layers, abc for the Na layers, and a’b’c’ for the Ni layers. text_images.description: A perspective three-dimensional ball-and-stick model enclosed by an inclined parallelepiped outlined with thin black lines. Axes at the lower left show a in red pointing roughly left, b in green pointing into the page, and c in blue pointing steeply toward the upper right. Three sphere sizes and colors represent the elements: the largest golden spheres are Na, medium silver-gray spheres are Ni, and the smallest red spheres are O. Thin cylindrical bonds are split between the colors of the connected atoms, such as yellow-red Na-O and silver-red Ni-O bonds. The structure is a highly ordered alternating layered arrangement along c. Silver-gray Ni layers lie near the upper and lower faces of the cell. Each Ni connects diagonally to 6 O atoms through 6 silver-red bonds, forming a typical $NiO_6$ octahedron. These edge-sharing octahedra extend laterally in planes perpendicular to c to form robust two-dimensional $NiO_2$ slabs. A layer of large golden Na spheres occupies the central plane in the open space between the 2 $NiO_2$ slabs. Each Na radiates 6 yellow-red bonds in an octahedral geometry, connecting upward to 3 O atoms at the bottom of the upper $NiO_2$ slab and downward to 3 O atoms at the top of the lower $NiO_2$ slab. Thus, rather than forming simple vertical linear units, the interlayer Na atoms act as structural anchors through a three-dimensional network of 6 contacts, 3 above and 3 below, joining the separated silver-red slabs along c into a continuous crystal network.

header:
Electrochemistry of an Oxidoreductase
Laccase is a copper-containing oxidoreductase that catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water while oxidizing phenolic compounds and various other substrates. Its catalytic center contains a T1 copper center (electron-acceptor site) and a T2/T3 trinuclear copper cluster (redox site). Because of its high activity and selectivity, laccase is often used as a cathode catalyst in biofuel cells. This problem concerns a laccase from Trametes versicolor, which may be approximated as a spherical protein with diameter d of approximately 5.0 nm. The standard electrode potential of its T1 copper center is $E_{\mathrm{T1}}^\circ=+0.78\ \mathrm{V}$ (vs. SHE). The laccase is immobilized on different electrodes to investigate its direct electron transfer (DET) and mediated electron transfer (MET) behavior.

header:
Problem 3 Solid Electrolyte Interphase
The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is an important research area in modern electrochemistry. During the first charging of a lithium-ion battery, the electrode potential lies below the reduction potential of the electrolyte, so additives and lithium salts in the electrolyte undergo electrochemical reductive decomposition at the solid-liquid interface. Insoluble solid products deposit on the electrode surface and form a passivation film that is electronically insulating but ionically conducting, thereby slowing electrode corrosion. Vinylene carbonate (VC), a classic film-forming additive, reacts preferentially and promotes formation of a high-quality SEI.

3.3.4 In the electrolyte, VC can also be electrochemically reduced to lithium oxalate and an enolate. Write the electrochemical reaction equation; EC participates in the reaction.

header:
Problem 1: What Is That Smell?
In 1803, the British chemist Tennant dissolved crude platinum in dilute aqua regia and found a small amount of black, insoluble powder remaining at the bottom of the vessel. Although early researchers regarded it merely as residual graphite, he suspected that it might contain unknown substances awaiting discovery. Through systematic alternating acid and base treatments, Tennant successfully separated the black residue into two new metallic elements, one of which is metal M. M was named for its distinctive odor and also has an extremely high density and numerous oxidation states.

Problem 6: Polysulfide Anions
A sodium-sulfur battery is a high-temperature molten secondary alkali-metal energy-storage battery that uses metallic sodium as the negative electrode, elemental sulfur as the positive electrode, and molten sodium beta-alumina as the solid electrolyte. It offers high energy density, inexpensive raw materials, and suitability for large-scale energy storage, and has become a research focus in electrochemical energy storage in recent years. Charging and discharging proceed through the formation of sodium polysulfides (Na_{2}S_{x}) with different chain lengths.

subquestions.text_open: 6.2 Sodium polysulfides (Na_{2}S_{x}) are key electroactive intermediates in sodium-sulfur batteries, and their anions can be synthesized and observed in the laboratory using common reagents. Under an N_{2} atmosphere, excess sodium tert-butoxide is added to a DMF solution of S_{8}, reducing S_{8} to polysulfide anion A. A disproportionates into another polysulfide anion B containing fewer atoms. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements show that some B anions undergo homolysis in solution to form bent anion C. C is trapped in zeolite cages in lazurite crystals, [(Na,Ca)_{4-8}(AlSiO_{4})_{6}(SO_{4},S,Cl)_{2}], and appears blue in solution. The sodium salt corresponding to polysulfide anion B is a common component of sodium-sulfur batteries. If it is heated to 300°C and melted, anion C dimerizes again to give isomer D of polysulfide anion B; the sulfur atoms in D occupy only two distinct chemical environments. 6.2.1 Give the chemical formulas of A and B.
6.2.2 Give the SMILES structures of C and D, showing the Lewis connectivity, and indicate the formal charge on every sulfur atom.

6.3 Anion C can also be observed when S_{8} is dissolved in liquid ammonia, together with another hydrogen-free anion E. Early studies proposed the following mechanism: first, liquid ammonia undergoes autoionization to form NH_{2}^{-} and NH_{4}^{+}; second, NH_{2}^{-} attacks S_{8}, giving S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} by addition; third, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} decomposes into cyclic anion F and a stable dibasic acid; fourth, F rearranges to form anion E and S_{8}, while the dibasic acid reacts with S_{8} and NH_{4}^{+} to form (NH_{4})_{2}S_{x}, which is subsequently converted into C. EPR measurements, however, show that anion F is not formed during the reaction. Moreover, the tendency of liquid ammonia to autoionize is extremely small and cannot explain the high solubility of S_{8} in liquid ammonia. Researchers therefore proposed a more plausible mechanism: first, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} and NH_{3} participate in a proton-transfer equilibrium, forming S_{8}NH_{3} while generating NH_{2}^{-}, which promotes dissolution; second, NH_{3} can also react by nucleophilic substitution to form the small molecule S_{2}NH_{3}; third, S_{8}NH_{2}^{-} decomposes to anion B and intermediate G; fourth, G transfers all of its protons to NH_{3} to form anion H; fifth, H reacts with S_{2}NH_{3} to give anion E and NH_{3}, with all species in this reaction having a stoichiometric coefficient of 1. 6.3.1 Give the SMILES structures of E, F, G, and H, showing the Lewis connectivity. The Lewis structure of E is known to contain two S-S single bonds, and its sulfur atoms occupy two distinct chemical environments.
6.3.2 In fact, the fifth reaction proceeds in three steps, and both the first and second steps generate SNH_{3}. Write the chemical equations for the three steps in order.

Calculations show that at 350℃ and 0.5 GPa, anion C can exist as a stable form of sulfur. Problem 9: Effects of Reaction Conditions and Mechanistic Investigation of Electrochemical Decarboxylative Alkylation
Electrochemical anodic oxidation can use inexpensive and readily available quaternary-ammonium salts of alkyl carboxylic acids as alkyl sources, avoiding the need for additional oxidants and transition-metal catalysts during decarboxylation. The method therefore offers a simple system, mild conditions, and environmental advantages. Researchers used an unsaturated amide as a model substrate to investigate decarboxylative methylation/arylation. Tetrabutylammonium acetate served as both the methyl source and electrolyte, with carbon cloth as the anode, platinum as the cathode, and DMSO as the solvent. Under constant-current electrolysis at 3 mA with 6.0 equivalents of acetic acid as a proton source at 70°C for 9 h (5.0 F/mol), the target oxindole was obtained in 80% yield.

Problem 1 Structural Chemistry of Aluminosilicates
The fundamental structural unit of silicates is the $[SiO_4]$ tetrahedron. Sharing corner oxygen atoms between silicate tetrahedra can form finite polynuclear anions, one-dimensional chains, two-dimensional layers, and three-dimensional infinite frameworks. Zeolite molecular sieves are aluminosilicates with regular channels and cage structures; their frameworks can be regarded as three-dimensional networks of corner-sharing $[SiO_4]$ and $[AlO_4]$ tetrahedra.

In its conventional unit cell, a sodalite cage (β cage) occupies each vertex and the body center, and the cages are connected by sharing hexagonal faces. In addition, each β cage is connected to other β cages by sharing square faces. Each β cage contains four sodium ions arranged as a regular tetrahedron, with a chloride ion at the center of the tetrahedron; each element has only one crystallographically distinct environment.

Problem 2 Fluoride-Ion-Selective Electrode
The core sensing element of a fluoride-ion-selective electrode is a LaF$_3$ single-crystal membrane doped with a small amount of Eu$^{2+}$ and sealed into the end of the electrode tube. The tube contains an internal reference solution, generally with fixed concentrations of NaF and NaCl, and an internal Ag/AgCl reference electrode. During doping, Eu$^{2+}$ replaces some La$^{3+}$ lattice sites, creating fluoride-ion vacancies to maintain electroneutrality. When the electrode is immersed in the sample solution, F$^{-}$ undergoes selective exchange at the membrane-solution interface and migrates through the crystal via these vacancies. Because the activities of F$^{-}$ differ across the membrane, the phase-boundary potentials on the two sides also differ; their difference is the membrane potential. Measuring this potential permits rapid and selective determination of fluoride in a sample. The structure is shown below.

Problem 6 Low-Valent Compounds of Group 13 Metals · II
Low-valent compounds of Group 13 elements such as aluminum, gallium, and indium (in the +1 oxidation state) have attracted widespread interest in synthetic chemistry and materials science because of their distinctive electronic structures and reactivities. These species often exist as oligomers, clusters, or coordination complexes. Their structural diversity arises from weak interactions between metal centers and their sensitivity to ligands. This problem focuses on the synthesis and structures of low-valent gallium and indium compounds and their coordination chemistry with Lewis acids, testing your understanding of cluster electron counting, aromaticity criteria, and coordination geometries.

Question 4 Determination of Iron by Titanium(III) Chloride–Potassium Dichromate Titration
Ferromanganese-silicon alloy is widely used as a deoxidizer and alloying additive in steelmaking, and its iron content strongly affects its quality. Potassium dichromate titration is a classical method for determining iron. After acid decomposition of the sample, titanium(III) chloride reduces $Fe^{3+}$ to $Fe^{2+}$; the solution is then titrated with standard potassium dichromate using sodium diphenylamine sulfonate as the indicator. This problem covers sample decomposition, prereduction, removal of interferences, and blank correction.

4.1 Sample decomposition

header:
The Ingenious Green Shoot
The heavy element M was first discovered by the British chemist William Crookes (1832-1919) while he was analyzing selenium-containing flue dust sent from a German sulfuric-acid factory. On observing through a spectroscope a bright emerald-green spectral line never seen before, he concluded that he had discovered a new element. Elemental M is silvery white and extremely soft, leaves a dark-gray streak on paper, and rapidly tarnishes when a freshly cut surface is exposed to air. M has two common oxidation states: the lower oxidation state is stable in aqueous solution, whereas compounds in the higher oxidation state readily decompose on heating and are strong oxidants.
When heated in air to approximately 300 °C, M burns to form black hygroscopic solid A. A dissolves in water to give a clear colorless solution containing the strong base B, whose aqueous basicity is close to that of KOH. Passing excess $CO_2$ through a solution of B precipitates colorless crystals C. Mixing C with nitric acid and potassium chromate solution gives yellow precipitate D (reaction 1). Adding hydrogen peroxide to a solution of B produces dark-brown powder E (reaction 2). Heating E with a KI solution acidified with hydrochloric acid gives yellow precipitate F and purple-black solid G (reaction 3). The mass fraction of M in F is 61.69 %.

header:
The Vanishing Sixfold Axis
Crystals in the hexagonal crystal system are characterized by a sixfold axis along the c direction. In addition to the simplest sixfold rotation axis, for which rotation by 60° about the axis brings the crystal into coincidence with itself, a crystal may contain either of the following two types of sixfold axes:
First, a $6_n$ screw axis, for which rotation by 60° followed by translation along c by n / 6 of the unit-cell length brings the crystal into coincidence with itself.
Second, a sixfold rotoinversion axis, for which rotation by 60° followed by inversion through a point on the axis brings the crystal into coincidence with itself.

header:
Chasing the Rainbow
A silvery-gray, high-melting metal M has no independent mineral in nature and occurs mainly in molybdenite. Industrially, molybdenite is roasted to concentrate the oxides of M.

subquestions.text_open: M forms numerous oxides in a wide range of oxidation states and colors, earning them the name "chemical rainbow." Oxide A contains M in its highest oxidation state. It is a yellow, highly deliquescent crystalline solid and dissolves in water to form a strong acid in which the mass fraction of M is 74.12%. Heating a mixture of A and elemental M in a sealed tube gives red crystals B with a metallic luster. Further heating to about 600 °C converts B into the blue solid M2O5; at still higher temperatures, M2O5 decomposes into the gray solid C. M has a different oxidation state in each of A, B, and C, and the oxidation state of M in C is the one most commonly found in oxides of its group. In the gas phase, the M atoms in A have tetrahedral coordination, whereas in the solid state A consists of corner-sharing octahedra and tetrahedra. Passing $Cl_2$ through a heated mixture of M powder and $KCl$ gives the red trimeric chloride D. 1.4 Thermodynamic data show that the reaction of C with $O_2$ to form B is spontaneous at 400 °C; experimentally, however, B decomposes at 400 °C by the reaction $3B(s)\rightarrow A(s)+C(s)$. Explain this apparent contradiction.

header:
Molecular Qubit Frameworks
Molecular qubit frameworks (MQFs) are among the leading candidate materials for quantum-information chips. Molecular qubits are functional materials that use electron-spin states within molecules to store and process quantum information. Under an applied magnetic field, two controllable quantum states can be selected from the low-energy levels of a magnetic center to serve as the qubit states "0" and "1". Long-term information storage requires minimizing environmental perturbations to the electron spins and isolating the magnetic centers from one another to obtain a long coherence time. A research team successfully constructed a diluted array of molecular spin qubits by doping trace amounts of $Nd^{3+}$ magnetic spin centers into a rigid yttrium-based MOF.

subquestions.text_open:

Each $C_2O_4^{2-}$ bridges two $Y^{3+}$ ions in a $\mu_2$-$\kappa^2$O,O′;$\kappa^2$O″,O‴ mode, chelating each $Y^{3+}$ ion through two O atoms. Answer the following questions about this compound.
2.1.1 The cation of this compound contains a six-membered ring, its two nitrogen atoms have identical chemical environments, and it contains no tertiary carbon atom. Write the SMILES string for the cation.
2.1.2 Give the coordination number of $Y^{3+}$.

2.3 In quantum-information storage, environmental lattice vibrations (phonon scattering) strongly perturb spin qubits and shorten their lifetimes. Theoretical studies show that, in this porous oxalate framework, the spin–lattice relaxation rate $1/T_1$ of $Nd^{3+}$ in the higher-temperature range 6.5K–8.5K is driven primarily by the combined Raman process and Orbach process and obeys the following kinetic equation:
$\frac{1}{T_1}=A_{Raman}T^7+A_{Orbach}\exp\left(-\frac{U_{eff}}{T}\right)$
Here, $A_{Raman}$ and $A_{Orbach}$ are the prefactors for the respective mechanisms, and $U_{eff}$ is the effective energy barrier of the low-lying excited state arising from strong spin–orbit coupling. The experimentally measured $U_{eff}$ for this material is 32.6 K.

Silver in the Making
In the worldview of alchemists, metals were not inert matter but substances that "grew" and "evolved" within Earth's crust. They believed that all base metals, such as lead and iron, were evolving toward the perfect noble metals, gold and silver. Metal M has the largest atomic number among elements with no definite year or person of discovery. As early as about 1500 CE, the Inca used M, Cu, and Sn to make alloys for the tumi knife.

Problem 2 Determination of Nickel by EDTA Titration
Nickel is an important strategic metal widely used in stainless steel, high-temperature alloys, and battery materials. Accurate determination of its content is essential for quality control. EDTA complexometric titration is commonly used to determine nickel, but the reaction between $Ni^{2+}$ and EDTA is slow. Back titration (adding excess EDTA first and then back-titrating with a standard $Cu^{2+}$ solution) is therefore often used to improve endpoint sensitivity. This problem concerns the preparation of standard solutions, the principle of back titration, and the elimination of interferences.

In addition, C reacts with an equimolar amount of CsF to give F; heating F converts it to G, in which the mass fraction of X is 23.91%.

Question 4 Determination of Aluminum by Titration (25 points, 10%)
Aluminum is an important component of light alloys, and its content directly affects strength, corrosion resistance, and processability. EDTA displacement titration is a classical method for determining aluminum. Excess EDTA is first added to complex aluminum ions, and the excess is back-titrated with standard zinc solution. Fluoride is then added to displace EDTA from Al–EDTA, and the released EDTA is titrated with standard zinc solution to determine the aluminum content.

subquestions.text_open:
4.1 Preparation of Standard Solutions. Disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA) solution (0.02 mol/L): Weigh 7.4448 g EDTA into a 400 mL beaker, dissolve in water, transfer to a 1000 mL volumetric flask, dilute to the mark, and mix. Standard zinc solution (0.02000 mol/L): Weigh 1.6276 g of zinc oxide (primary standard reagent) that has been dried to constant mass at 110 ℃ into a 400 mL beaker. Add 20 mL hydrochloric acid (1 + 1) and heat to dissolve. Add approximately 200 mL water and then add aqueous ammonia (1 + 1) dropwise until Congo red paper changes from blue to violet. Cool, transfer to a 1000 mL volumetric flask, dilute to the mark with water, and mix. 4.2 Dissolution of the Sample. Accurately weigh 1.0008 g of the alloy sample into a 400 mL glass beaker. Add 20 mL~30 mL hydrochloric acid (1 + 1) and heat to dissolve; for samples that are difficult to dissolve, an appropriate amount of concentrated hydrochloric acid or concentrated nitric acid may be added. Add 5 mL concentrated nitric acid dropwise for oxidation, then add 10 mL~30 mL sulfuric acid (1 + 1). Evaporate until sulfuric acid fumes have evolved for 1 min. Remove from heat and cool slightly, add 50 mL water, and heat to dissolve the salts. 4.3 Separation of the Precipitate. Acidity adjustment: Add 100 mL of complexing-agent solution (containing 200 g/L ammonium citrate and 25 g/L ammonium oxalate) to the test solution, and adjust the pH to 4~5 with aqueous ammonia (1 + 1) and sulfuric acid (1 + 8). If a precipitate forms in a tungsten-containing sample, first add concentrated aqueous ammonia until basic and heat to dissolve the tungstic acid precipitate. After cooling, adjust the pH to 4~5 with sulfuric acid (1 + 1) and aqueous ammonia (1 + 1). If the test solution is turbid, heat it to boiling until clear, cool, and readjust the pH to 4~5. Precipitation and dissolution: Transfer the test solution to a 400 mL plastic beaker, add a small amount of paper pulp, and add 100 mL sodium fluoride solution (35 g/L) with stirring. Stir thoroughly for 5 min and let stand for 40 min. Filter through slow filter paper containing a small amount of paper pulp, wash 7~8 times with sodium fluoride solution (5 g/L), and discard the filtrate. Return the precipitate and filter paper to the original glass beaker and immediately add 20 mL hydrochloric acid-boric acid mixed acid (boric acid:hydrochloric acid:water = 15:25:60) to dissolve the precipitate; it must be added immediately, or complete dissolution will be difficult. Add 20 mL~25 mL concentrated nitric acid and boil without covering with a watch glass to destroy the filter paper. Cool slightly, add 7 mL concentrated perchloric acid, and heat to near dryness with fuming. Cool slightly and add 50 mL water to dissolve the salts.
4.3.3 Write the ionic equation for addition of sodium fluoride in the “Separation of the Precipitate” step. The purpose of adding paper pulp during filtration is (select one).
A. Increase precipitate purity
B. Loosen the gelatinous precipitate and prevent passage through the filter
C. Act as an indicator
D. Adsorb impurity ions
4.3.4 Write the ionic equation for dissolution of the precipitate by the hydrochloric acid–boric acid mixture.

4.4 Titration
Accurately add 20.00 mL EDTA solution to the test solution and boil for 2–3 min. Add 2 drops of 2,4-dinitrophenol solution (2 g/L), then add ammonia (1 + 1) dropwise until the solution is pale yellow. Continue boiling for 1–2 min and cool; if the yellow color fades, add ammonia dropwise until pale yellow again. Add 20 mL acetate–ammonium acetate buffer (pH 5.0–5.5) and 4 drops of xylenol orange solution (2 g/L). Titrate with standard zinc solution until violet-red, without recording the reading. Add 1–2 g sodium fluoride, boil for 2–3 min, and cool to room temperature. If the solution is violet-red, add hydrochloric acid (1 + 1) dropwise until the color just disappears. Add another 10 mL acetate–ammonium acetate buffer and 1–2 drops of xylenol orange solution. Titrate with standard zinc solution to a violet-red endpoint; 12.66 mL is consumed.
4.4.1 Does the EDTA solution require standardization in this experiment? Briefly explain.
4.4.2 Write the ionic equation for addition of sodium fluoride followed by boiling, using $H_2Y^{2-}$ for the doubly charged ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion.

Problem 6 Determination of the Oxygen-Uptake Ratio of an Oxygen Carrier (23 points, 10%)
A laboratory has prepared inactive Co(Salen) and wishes to determine the oxygen-uptake ratio $n_{O_2}:n_{[Co(II)(Salen)]}$ after the carrier has fully absorbed $O_2$ from its surroundings under specified conditions. Inactive Co(Salen) itself has almost no oxygen-uptake capacity, but it dissolves in coordinating solvents such as DMF or DMSO, and the resulting solution can absorb oxygen. The main procedure is described below:

header_images.description: Schematic apparatus for measuring the oxygen-uptake ratio, with no text, letters, numbers, or arrow labels. At left is a U-shaped gas burette. Its left arm is vertical and bears evenly spaced short, unnumbered graduations. Both arms contain liquid, with the level in the left arm higher than that in the right. In the center is a three-neck round-bottom flask containing liquid in its lower portion and resting above a rectangular base. The left neck connects to a downward-sloping bent addition tube that also contains liquid; its liquid level lies below that in the flask, and its downward-facing open end is not submerged. The middle neck connects to a long vertical tube that bends left at the top and enters the right arm of the gas burette; this connecting tube contains no liquid. The right neck connects to a two-way stopcock assembly with a spherical bulb above it, a short tube at the top, and two symmetric thin rods; this part contains no liquid.

subquestions.text_open:
6.1 Assembly of the Measurement Apparatus. Accurately weigh 0.1136 g Co(Salen) and transfer it through a dry glass funnel into a clean, dry three-neck flask. Assemble the apparatus as shown below. Apply a layer of petroleum jelly, as thin as possible, to the ground-glass joints of the bent tube, gas inlet tube, and two-way stopcock. Place 5 mL DMF (or DMSO) in the bent tube and connect the charging bent tube to the flask. Use a narrow-tip glass dropper to add 1 mL deionized water to the gas burette, whose graduations increase upward. Inflate the oxygen bag and connect it to the two-way stopcock on the right. Apply pressure to the oxygen bag so that air is expelled through the graduated gas burette. When the oxygen in the bag has been almost completely discharged, close the stopcock. Add approximately 5 mL more deionized water to the graduated gas burette so that the difference between the liquid levels exceeds 2 cm. Observe the liquid levels; the system may be considered to have reached thermal equilibrium when the change in liquid level is less than 0.03 mL over three consecutive minutes.
6.2 Determination of the Oxygen-Uptake Ratio
After assembling the apparatus, determine the oxygen-uptake ratio of the Co(Salen) sample as follows.
Record the laboratory temperature and atmospheric pressure. Remove the oxygen bag, open the stopcock to the atmosphere, and keep the gas burette vertical. When the liquid levels in the two arms are equal (difference less than 0.03 mL), close the stopcock and record the position of the liquid level in the gas burette. Then introduce DMF (or DMSO) into the flask, stir rapidly, and observe the changes in the reactants. Promptly add deionized water to the gas burette with a narrow-tip glass dropper to keep the liquid levels in its two arms equal. Record the liquid-level position every 20~40 seconds until ________. Calculate the actual volume of oxygen absorbed.
